A citywide result tells us whether a measure passed. Geographic results can show how support varied across the city—and give us a baseline for following where investment goes next.

::: {.callout-note title="Reading geographic coverage"}
Geographic records are added only after their certified counts and reporting scope have been checked. Maps also require matching boundaries and complete-coverage checks. An unavailable result is not a zero vote.
:::

## What the comparison can tell us

The first comparison will connect support for a spending measure with documented allocations, awards, and expenditures. It will ask where support was strongest, which communities received investment, and what public records explain the priorities.

**Support is not a test of who deserves investment.** Communities voting against a measure can still have substantial needs. Differences between voting patterns and spending locations are questions to investigate, not proof of favoritism.

## Precincts are not neighborhoods

A precinct is an election reporting unit. A neighborhood is a different geography. Before publishing neighborhood-level estimates, this project will document how those boundaries align and whether any allocation introduces uncertainty. A precinct crossing neighborhood boundaries does not reveal how each neighborhood’s residents voted.

Early, mail, provisional, and election-day votes must also be reconciled. Records reported separately from precincts will remain clearly identified rather than being assigned to places without evidence.
